issues.legal_issue: A court may set aside an execution sale for irregularity or fraud only when the applicant proves both the irregularity or fraud and substantial injury caused by it.
material_facts: The judgment debtor applied to set aside a sale of immovable property conducted in execution of a money decree.
The application alleged defects in the sale process and that the property would have fetched a higher price.
issues.conclusion: Proof of a material irregularity or fraud alone is insufficient; the applicant must also establish substantial injury caused by that irregularity or fraud.
issues.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 90(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires substantial injury caused by a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting an execution sale. The Court relied on Saheb Khan v. Mohd. Yousufuddin, which applied this requirement, and referred to Dhirendra Nath Gorai v. Sudhir Chandra Ghosh, Jaswantlal Natvarlal Thakkar v. Sushilaben Manilal Dangarwala, and Kadiyala Rama Rao v. Gutala Kahna Rao.

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A person affected by an immovable-property sale conducted in execution of a decree applies to have that sale set aside.
predicates.material_sale_irregularity: The applicant proves a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the execution sale.
predicates.sale_fraud: The applicant proves fraud in publishing or conducting the execution sale.
predicates.substantial_injury_caused_by_irregularit: The applicant proves substantial injury caused by the material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale.

issues.definition: When an execution sale is challenged, the sale may be set aside only if a material irregularity or fraud is proved and that defect caused substantial injury.

issues.legal_issue: The sale was not liable to be set aside because the objections did not establish a material irregularity or fraud causing substantial injury.
material_facts: The executing court found the debtor's objections to the sale procedure and price unsupported and dismissed the application to set aside the sale.
The sale proclamation was issued sufficiently before the sale, and the Supreme Court treated the period as running from the date the proclamation order was issued.
The record showed publicity by newspaper and beat of drums, and seven bidders participated in the auction.
The sale papers disclosed valuations, and the debtor produced no evidence or bidder offering a higher price than the auction bid.
The debtor did not raise a plea of fraud.
issues.conclusion: The debtor had not made out a ground under Order 21 Rule 90(2) to set aside the sale. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and restored the executing court's order dismissing the application.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 21 Rules 64 and 66 to 68 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the sale must follow the prescribed procedure. Order 21 Rule 67(1), read with Rule 54(2), provides for publication of the proclamation by a customary mode, including beat of drum, and by affixing copies at specified places; newspaper publication requires a specific court direction. Applying Order 21 Rule 90(2) and Saheb Khan v. Mohd. Yousufuddin, the Court held that the sale could not be set aside without a material irregularity or fraud that caused substantial injury. It found the objections meritless on the evidence and distinguished the other cases cited by the debtor on their facts.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and sale_procedure_complied and notice_period_sufficient and adequate_sale_publicity and multiple_bidders_participated and sale_valuations_disclosed and no_evidence_of_higher_value and not fraud_pleaded

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A judgment debtor applies to set aside an immovable-property auction sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.sale_procedure_complied: The executing court follows the prescribed procedure for settling and publishing the sale proclamation and conducting the sale.
predicates.notice_period_sufficient: The sale is fixed sufficiently after the order issuing the proclamation, when the notice period is counted from that order.
predicates.adequate_sale_publicity: The sale is publicized by the means used in the locality and in any other manner required by the court's directions.
predicates.multiple_bidders_participated: More than one bidder participates in the auction after the sale is publicized.
predicates.sale_valuations_disclosed: The sale documents disclose valuations of the property to prospective bidders.
predicates.no_evidence_of_higher_value: The debtor produces no evidence supporting the claimed higher market value or showing that a higher price could have been obtained at the sale.
predicates.fraud_pleaded: The debtor does not allege fraud in publishing or conducting the sale.

issues.definition: When a debtor challenges an execution sale, compliance with the sale procedure and notice requirements, adequate publicity, bidder participation, disclosed valuations, no evidence supporting a higher value, and no fraud allegation support leaving the sale in place.
